criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking-water and sanitation service access across Brazil's Legal Amazon (state-level household water and sewer network connection rates) and in four Amazonian case studies (Iauaretê, São Gabriel da Cachoeira, Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve, and Manaus).
criterion_notes.c2: Fails BOTH the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, no rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules governing connection or disconnection, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure) is empirically examined; passing descriptive references to a flat R$ 9.00 monthly fee and popular resistance to volumetric billing in São Gabriel da Cachoeira (citing Giatti 2007), private concessionaire operation in Manaus (Águas do Amazonas), Portaria 518/2004 water-quality standards, and general concluding remarks on cost-recovery difficulties in non-monetized communities are incidental background rather than an analyzed determinant of access. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper also fails (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because its explicit analytical scope and empirical focus are environmental/hydrological conditions, macro-economic and demographic growth (GDP per capita and urbanization), infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural beliefs, perceptions, and hygiene/water-use practices rather than any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor.
criterion_notes.c3: Presents descriptive secondary empirical analysis of IBGE/PNAD state-level indicators (2002-2009 GDP per capita growth and household water/sewer network coverage, plus 2008 IBGE municipal environmental perception data) combined with a narrative multi-case synthesis summarizing empirical findings (household surveys, microbiological water testing, and parasitological data) from four previously published case studies in Amazonas State.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports relevant service access outcomes, including the percentage of permanent private households connected to public water supply and sewage networks across Legal Amazon states, population lacking public water access or facing precarious supply in Manaus, and household water sources used (wells, rainwater, river water, public taps, piped network) across case-study sites.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (9 Legal Amazon states and permanent private households in IBGE/PNAD data; communities and surveyed households across four Amazonas case studies), examined non-legal exposures (GDP per capita growth, urbanization, environmental/seasonal conditions, infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural perceptions/practices), water/sanitation access outcomes, and study design (descriptive ecological secondary-data analysis plus narrative synthesis of previously published case studies) are identifiable from the text, confirming wrong exposure (E03).
criterion_notes.c6: Published in Portuguese, an eligible language without translation under Criterion 9.

evidence_quotes.quote: Nesse sentido, são objetivos do presente artigo identificar aspectos atuais da situação de acesso a água para consumo humano, bem como enriquecer o debate sobre os desafios para o atendimento das necessidades humanas por água na Amazônia Brasileira, considerando em distintas escalas espaciais, aspectos de infraestrutura e a necessidade de se compreender dinâmicas socioculturais.

Em um panorama regional verificamos um sério déficit para a Amazônia Legal, sendo que o percentual de domicílios permanentes ligados à rede de abastecimento de água na região em 2009 foi de 58,5%, bastante inferior ao nacional no mesmo ano (83,1%). De modo mais alarmante consta o percentual de domicílios em estados amazônicos com ligação à rede de esgotos sanitários, que em 2009 foi de apenas 9,4%, enquanto o nacional figurou 52,5%.

Este estudo tem como objetivo explorar condicionantes de acesso à água para consumo humano, considerando aspectos ambientais, socioculturais e de infraestrutura. Para isso, analisam-se: a precária cobertura por saneamento básico na região, por meio de macroindicadores; e estudos de caso em distintas escalas espaciais: comunidade indígena; cidade de pequeno porte, comunidades ribeirinhas, e uma cidade de grande porte, Manaus, maior centro urbano da Amazônia Pan-Amazônica.
Não havia cobrança proporcional à vazão de água utilizada por domicílio, simplesmente cobrava-se valor fixo mensal de R$ 9,00 por ligação, fato que incidia grandes desperdícios de água aduzida;
Nessas condições, 600 mil habitantes permaneciam em situação de abastecimento precário, enquanto 250 mil não tinham acesso à água de abastecimento público (ÁGUAS DO AMAZONAS, 2007).

raw_response.exposure: Macro-economic and demographic dynamics (state GDP per capita growth, rapid urbanization/migration), environmental/hydrological characteristics (river water types, seasonal floodplain cycles, landfill groundwater contamination), sanitation infrastructure deficits, and sociocultural beliefs, taboos, and health perceptions.
raw_response.outcome: Percentage of permanent private households connected to public water supply and sewage networks (2002-2009); population without public water supply or with precarious supply; household drinking-water source selection (wells, rainwater, river, public taps, piped network), household water treatment, fecal/chemical contamination, and intestinal parasitoses.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Nine states of Brazil's Legal Amazon (total population 25,474,365 in 2010; permanent private households in IBGE PNAD 2002-2009) and summarized previously published case studies in Amazonas State: Distrito de Iauaretê (~2,700 inhabitants, 65 water samples), São Gabriel da Cachoeira (~18,000 urban / 39,129 municipal inhabitants), 4 riverine communities in Mamirauá Sustainable Development Reserve (~350 inhabitants), and Manaus (1,802,014 inhabitants, including household surveys of n=296 in Santa Etelvina and n=162 in Novo Israel).
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While the article examines household and community drinking-water and sanitation access in Brazil's Legal Amazon using secondary IBGE macro-indicators and a synthesis of four previously published case studies in Amazonas State, its examined determinants are economic growth (GDP per capita), urbanization, environmental/hydrological conditions, infrastructure gaps, and sociocultural beliefs, perceptions, and practices. It does not empirically examine a legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor under either the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope or the plain wording of Criterion 2 (incidental mentions of a flat R$ 9.00 monthly fee and resistance to volumetric charging in São Gabriel da Cachoeira, private concessionaire operation in Manaus, Portaria 518/2004 potability limits, and general concluding remarks on cost recovery and health education are descriptive context rather than an analyzed governance or rule-type exposure).
raw_response.study_design: Descriptive ecological analysis of secondary macro-indicators (IBGE/PNAD 2002-2009) combined with a narrative multi-case overview synthesizing four previously published empirical case studies.
